clinicalPearls: Second most common cause of congenital adrenal hyperplasia after 21-hydroxylase deficiency, arising from biallelic pathogenic variants in CYP11B1.
The classic phenotype combines androgen excess (virilisation) with hypertension, distinguishing it from the salt-wasting seen in 21-hydroxylase deficiency.
Enzyme block prevents conversion of 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol and of 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC) to corticosterone, so both precursors accumulate.
Accumulated 11-deoxycorticosterone has intrinsic mineralocorticoid activity, driving sodium retention, volume expansion and low-renin, low-potassium hypertension.
Loss of cortisol negative feedback raises ACTH, which stimulates adrenal androgen synthesis and produces prenatal virilisation of 46,XX infants.
46,XX newborns typically present with ambiguous genitalia; 46,XY infants may appear normal at birth and present later with precocious pseudo-puberty and rapid growth.
Hypertension is often absent in the neonatal period and emerges over infancy and childhood, so a normal early blood pressure does not exclude the diagnosis.
A non-classic (late-onset) form with milder enzyme impairment presents with hyperandrogenism, acne and menstrual disturbance without significant hypertension.
reference.pathophysiology: 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder of adrenal steroidogenesis caused by loss-of-function variants in CYP11B1, the gene encoding the mitochondrial enzyme that catalyses the final step of cortisol synthesis in the zona fasciculata. Impaired hydroxylation blocks conversion of 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol and of 11-deoxycorticosterone to corticosterone, so these two upstream precursors accumulate to high concentrations. Because 11-deoxycorticosterone is a potent mineralocorticoid, its excess causes sodium and water retention, plasma volume expansion, suppression of renin and aldosterone, potassium loss and hypertension, which paradoxically coexists with a deficiency of true aldosterone. The failure of cortisol production removes negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, raising corticotrophin, which drives adrenal hyperplasia and shunts precursors into the intact androgen pathway; the resulting excess of adrenal androgens virilises the external genitalia of affected 46,XX fetuses in utero and causes postnatal androgen effects in both sexes. The distinct CYP11B2 gene encoding aldosterone synthase in the zona glomerulosa is preserved, but its activity is downregulated by the volume expansion, explaining the characteristic low-renin state.

Serum androgens including androstenedione and testosterone

CYP11B1 molecular genetic testing to confirm diagnosis and guide family counselling

redFlags: Neonate with ambiguous genitalia requiring urgent endocrine and multidisciplinary assessment
Adrenal crisis with hypotension, vomiting and hypoglycaemia during intercurrent illness despite the hypertensive phenotype
Accelerated growth with advancing bone age indicating uncontrolled androgen excess
Severe or difficult-to-control hypertension with hypokalaemia
Signs of hypertensive end-organ damage such as retinopathy or left ventricular hypertrophy in a child
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis, glucocorticoid replacement to suppress excess precursor and androgen production, and control of blood pressure, growth and pubertal outcomes are generally favourable. Prognosis is worsened by delayed diagnosis, long-standing hypertension with end-organ damage, and complications of over- or under-treatment such as impaired final height or iatrogenic Cushingoid features.
pitfalls: Assuming all congenital adrenal hyperplasia causes salt wasting; 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency instead causes hypertension and sodium retention.
Expecting hypertension at birth; it commonly develops later, so its absence in a neonate does not exclude the diagnosis.
Overlooking the risk of adrenal crisis because the child is hypertensive, when glucocorticoid deficiency still predisposes to decompensation during stress.
Missing the non-classic form in adolescents or women presenting only with hyperandrogenism and mistaking it for polycystic ovary syndrome.
Failing to titrate glucocorticoid dose to avoid both androgen breakthrough and iatrogenic hypercortisolism during growth.

management: Glucocorticoid replacement (hydrocortisone in children) to restore cortisol and suppress ACTH-driven adrenal androgen and 11-deoxycorticosterone excess
Control the low-renin hypertension with mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists to counter deoxycorticosterone-mediated mineralocorticoid effect and correct hypokalaemia
Stress-dose glucocorticoid escalation during intercurrent illness, surgery or trauma, with parenteral hydrocortisone for adrenal crisis
Individualised surgical and psychological management of atypical genitalia in affected 46,XX infants, with careful discussion of timing
Monitor growth, bone age, pubertal progression, blood pressure and adrenal precursor and androgen markers to titrate the glucocorticoid dose and avoid over-treatment
Coordinate care through paediatric endocrinology, urology and clinical psychology
Educate the family on sick-day rules and provide an emergency parenteral steroid kit
Offer genetic counselling and CYP11B1 family testing, with discussion of prenatal diagnosis options
